ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached diagram is a 6 by 6 square grid. The shaded green squares are in the top row columns 2 and 3, and in the second row column 3. Reasoning: To make the design, including the square grid, have 4 axes of symmetry, the shaded-square pattern must be symmetric across the vertical middle line, horizontal middle line, main diagonal, and anti-diagonal. Therefore every initially shaded square forces all squares in its full orbit under the 8 symmetries of the square. For the shaded square at row 1, column 2, its orbit has 8 cells. For the shaded square at row 1, column 3, its orbit also has 8 cells and is disjoint from the first orbit. For the shaded square at row 2, column 3, its orbit also has 8 cells and is disjoint from the other two orbits. So the final symmetric design must contain 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 shaded squares. Since 3 squares are already shaded, the number that must be added is 24 - 3 = 21.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as a 6 by 6 square grid with three initially shaded cells: top row columns 2 and 3, and second row column 3. From the text, the goal is to add the fewest shaded squares so that the whole shaded-cell pattern, together with the square grid, has 4 axes of symmetry. Use the fact that a square grid can have exactly these 4 axes: vertical middle line, horizontal middle line, main diagonal, and anti-diagonal. For each initially shaded cell, generate all cells forced by reflecting it across these four axes, equivalently take its full orbit under the 8 symmetries of the square. The cell at row 1 column 2 forces 8 cells total; row 1 column 3 forces another disjoint set of 8; row 2 column 3 forces another disjoint set of 8. Thus the final symmetric design must contain 24 shaded cells. Since 3 are already shaded, the smallest number to add is 24 - 3 = 21.
